passages.t: Persia, and a mighty king of Greece
passages.happening:
The messenger continues. In the first year of Darius the Mede he had stood up to strengthen and protect him (verse 1). ‘Now then, I will tell you the truth’ (verse 2). Three more kings will arise in Persia, and then a fourth, far richer than the rest, who will stir up everyone against the kingdom of Greece.

‘Then a mighty king will arise, who will rule with great authority and do as he pleases’ (verse 3). But as soon as he is established, his kingdom will be broken up and divided toward the four winds of heaven. It will not go to his descendants, and it will not have his authority. It will be uprooted and given to others (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is the heart of the final vision. The messenger said he would tell Daniel what is written in the Book of Truth, and now he does, in more detail than any other prophecy in the Old Testament.

Most interpreters of every school agree that verses 2 to 35 match the history of the fourth to second centuries BC closely. The fourth rich king of Persia is often identified as Xerxes I, who invaded Greece in 480 BC. The mighty king is Alexander the Great. His empire was divided among his generals after his death in 323 BC, and his own sons did not inherit it.

The chapter narrows the focus of the earlier visions. Chapters 2 and 7 surveyed a sequence of empires, and chapter 8 focused on Persia, Greece and a little horn. Chapter 11 follows the Greek period king by king until it reaches the ruler who attacks God's people and temple. That crisis, and the faithfulness it demands, is where the whole book has been heading.
passages.later: Chapter 8 had pictured the same king as a goat's great horn: ‘at the height of his power, his large horn was broken off, and four prominent horns came up in its place’ (Daniel 8:8). And Esther tells of life under one of those rich Persian kings, Xerxes, in ‘the citadel of Susa’ (Esther 1:2).
passages.asks: The mighty king did as he pleased, and his kingdom went to others. Ask what you are building that you assume will last after you. And ask how it changes your use of power to know that it is lent.

passages.t: The kings of the South and the North
passages.happening:
Now the vision follows two lines of kings. ‘The king of the South will grow strong, but one of his commanders will grow even stronger and will rule his own kingdom with great authority’ (verse 5). After some years they make an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the South goes to the king of the North to seal it. But she will not keep her position, and she will be given up with those who brought her (verse 6).

A branch from her family rises up, attacks the king of the North and carries off his gods and treasures to Egypt (verses 7-9). The northern king's sons gather great armies (verse 10). The two kings fight back and forth, with great armies raised and swept away (verses 11-15). The king of the North stands in the Beautiful Land with destruction in his hand (verse 16). He gives a daughter in marriage to overthrow the southern kingdom, ‘but his plan will not succeed or help him’ (verse 17). He turns to the coastlands, but a commander puts an end to his insolence, and he stumbles and falls (verses 18-19).

‘In his place one will arise who will send out a tax collector for the glory of the kingdom’ (verse 20), and within a few days he will be destroyed.
passages.hearers:
The king of the South is the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt. The king of the North is the Seleucid dynasty in Syria and Mesopotamia. Judea, the Beautiful Land, lay between them and was fought over for more than a century.

The details are close to the history readers on all sides recognize. The commander who grew stronger is Seleucus I. The daughter sent north is Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, married to Antiochus II around 252 BC and later murdered with her child. Her brother Ptolemy III avenged her and carried off Seleucid treasures. Antiochus III, the Great, lost at Raphia in 217 BC but won at Panium around 200 BC, bringing Judea under Seleucid rule. He married his daughter Cleopatra I to Ptolemy V, was defeated by the Romans in 190 BC and died in 187 BC. His son Seleucus IV sent his minister to seize temple funds.

The first hearers, who lived under these kings, were being told that the wars that tossed their land back and forth were known to God. The kings did as they pleased, made marriages and broke them, and still the end came at the appointed time.
passages.later: Isaiah had said the same of an earlier empire: God would punish the king of Assyria ‘for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes’ (Isaiah 10:12). And a psalm promises, ‘Those who know Your name trust in You’ (Psalm 9:10), whoever rules.
passages.asks: For more than a century, God's people lived in the land the great powers fought over. Ask what it means to be faithful when you are caught between forces much larger than you. And ask where you have treated people as the kings here treated their daughters, as pieces in a plan.

passages.happening:
‘In his place a despicable person will arise; royal honors will not be given to him, but he will come in a time of peace and seize the kingdom by intrigue’ (verse 21). Armies are swept away before him, ‘along with a prince of the covenant’ (verse 22). He acts deceitfully and rises to power with only a few people (verse 23). In a time of peace he invades the richest provinces and lavishes plunder on his followers (verse 24).

He stirs up his power against the king of the South, who falls by the plots devised against him (verses 25-26). ‘And the two kings, with their hearts bent on evil, will speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for still the end will come at the appointed time’ (verse 27).

The king of the North returns home with great wealth, ‘but his heart will be set against the holy covenant’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The despicable person is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who took the throne in 175 BC though he was not the heir. Readers of every school agree on this much. The prince of the covenant is widely identified with the high priest Onias III. Antiochus invaded Egypt in 169 BC and plundered the Jerusalem temple on his way home.

The picture of two kings lying to each other at the same table is sharp. Power in this chapter is mostly deceit. And the line still the end will come at the appointed time comes back again and again in these verses. Whatever the kings plot, God has set the time.

The first hearers under Antiochus knew this man. They were being shown that his rise, his tricks and his wealth had been seen beforehand, and that his time was measured.
passages.later: Chapter 8 had described the same king: ‘an insolent king, skilled in intrigue, will come to the throne’ (Daniel 8:23). The book of Psalms says, ‘the LORD frustrates the plans of the nations’ (Psalm 33:10).
passages.asks: The two kings spoke lies at the same table. Ask where deceit has become normal in the places of power you know. And ask what it means for you that, whatever they plot, the end comes at the appointed time.

passages.t: The abomination, and those who know their God
passages.happening:
At the appointed time the king invades the South again, but this time is different (verse 29). ‘Ships of Kittim will come against him, and he will lose heart’ (verse 30). He turns back and rages against the holy covenant, and favors those who forsake it.

‘His forces will rise up and desecrate the temple fortress. They will abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation’ (verse 31). With flattery he corrupts those who violate the covenant, ‘but the people who know their God will firmly resist him’ (verse 32).

‘Those with insight will instruct many, though for a time they will fall by sword or flame, or be captured or plundered’ (verse 33). When they fall they will get a little help, but many will join them insincerely (verse 34). ‘Some of the wise will fall, so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless until the time of the end, for it will still come at the appointed time’ (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
On a second campaign in 168 BC, a Roman envoy arriving by ship ordered Antiochus out of Egypt. Kittim here means the Romans. Humiliated, he turned on Jerusalem. In 167 BC he banned Jewish worship and set up a pagan altar in the temple, recorded in 1 Maccabees 1:54 in the very words of the Greek Daniel, the abomination of desolation. The little help of verse 34 is often taken as the Maccabean revolt.

The chapter divides the people into two kinds. Some forsake the covenant and are won over by flattery. Others know their God and stand firm. Among these are the wise, maskilim in Hebrew, those with insight, who teach many. The book itself seems written for them.

The chapter is honest about what faithfulness cost. Some of the wise fell by sword and flame. The book does not promise they will escape. It says their suffering refines them, and that the end will come at the appointed time. The answer to their deaths comes in chapter 12.
passages.later: Jesus took up the phrase as he foretold the destruction of the temple, speaking of ‘the abomination of desolation,’ described by the prophet Daniel (Matthew 24:15). And Zechariah speaks of the refining of God's people: ‘I will refine them like silver and test them like gold’ (Zechariah 13:9).
passages.hard:
Does God want his people to suffer so that they will be refined?

Verse 35 says some of the wise will fall so that they may be refined, purified and made spotless. In its setting it is a word to people already suffering for their faith under a persecutor, telling them that their suffering is not wasted and that God sets its limit. It does not say that God takes pleasure in it, and it does not make the persecutor right. The same chapter calls him despicable, and the next chapter promises that the faithful dead will rise.

It is not a word to say to someone else who is suffering, and it gives no one a warrant to call another person's suffering a good thing, or to cause it. These notes do not read any reader's suffering as a test they are failing.
passages.asks: The people who know their God stood firm, and the wise taught many even when it cost them. Ask what it would look like for you to know your God in that way. And ask whom you are helping to understand, as the wise did.

passages.t: The king who exalts himself, and his end
passages.happening:
‘Then the king will do as he pleases and will exalt and magnify himself above every god, and he will speak monstrous things against the God of gods’ (verse 36). He will succeed until the time of wrath is complete, for what has been decreed must be done.

He will show no regard for the gods of his fathers, nor for the one desired by women, nor for any god, because he will magnify himself above them all (verse 37). He honors a god of fortresses instead, with gold and silver and precious stones (verse 38), and rewards those who acknowledge him (verse 39).

‘At the time of the end’ the king of the South engages him, and the king of the North storms out with chariots, horsemen and ships, sweeping through many countries like a flood (verse 40). He enters the Beautiful Land. Egypt does not escape, and the Libyans and Cushites submit (verses 41-43). But news from the east and north alarms him, and he goes out in fury to destroy (verse 44).

‘He will pitch his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain, but he will meet his end with no one to help him’ (verse 45).
passages.hearers:
The king who magnifies himself above every god is the climax of the book's long line of proud rulers: Nebuchadnezzar on his roof, Belshazzar at his feast, the little horn with its boastful mouth. Each claimed what belongs to God, and each was brought down.

The last line is the point the first hearers most needed. The persecutor will meet his end with no one to help him. However great his power, it is limited and it will end.

How to read these verses is debated, and the hard question below sets out the views. Verses 40 to 45 describe a final campaign in Egypt and a death between the sea and the holy mountain, which do not match what is known of Antiochus's death in Persia in 164 BC.
passages.later: Paul describes the coming opponent of God in words close to verse 36: ‘He will oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship’ (2 Thessalonians 2:4). And Isaiah had pictured the fall of Babylon's proud king, who said, ‘I will make myself like the Most High’ (Isaiah 14:14).
passages.hard:
Who is the king of verses 36 to 45?

The precision of verses 2 to 35 is at the center of the debate over Daniel's date. The critical view holds that the chapter was written during Antiochus IV's persecution, about 167 to 164 BC, surveying past history in the form of prophecy, as other Jewish apocalypses did. Because verses 40 to 45 do not match Antiochus's death in Persia, these scholars read them as a real prediction written shortly before he died.

The traditional view holds that God revealed this history to Daniel in the sixth century BC. Many who hold it, following an approach found already in Jerome, see the text passing beyond Antiochus at some point, often at verse 36, to a final opponent of God, with Antiochus as a foreshadowing. The dispensational view reads verses 36 to 45 as a future ruler in the last days, with the kings of the North and South as powers of that time. Interpreters in that school differ over who those powers will be, and the text itself names no modern nation.

These notes take no side. They identify no person, nation or movement of the present day with the king of the North, the king of the South, or the king who exalts himself. Every view agrees on what the chapter asks of its readers: that the people who know their God should stand firm, teach others and trust that the persecutor will meet his end with no one to help him.
passages.asks: The proudest king in the book ends with no one to help him. Ask where you are tempted to magnify yourself, even in small ways. And ask whether you can trust, while powerful people boast, that their end has been set.
